title: Run JoinDependentFilterRule before DistributivityRule
summary: In src/optimizer/optimizer.cpp I moved the JoinDependentFilterRule registration to just before DistributivityRule. Nothing else changed. Before, DistributivityRule pulled the shared join-key equality out of the root OR first, so JoinDependentFilterRule never saw an OR and derived no per-table filters. With the new order it derives the per-table OR filters, and they get pushed down to the scans. The build is OK and bench results match. Bench, best vs mine: q19 378→204ms (-45.9%), then 353→185ms (-47.6%) on a rerun. Visible geomean -4.6%. No other template moved beyond noise. q04 showed +5.5% and +5.1% on two runs, then -3.6% on a third. q04 has no OR predicate, so the rule cannot touch its plan, which means this is noise. I did not run the optimizer unit tests (test/optimizer/*) or plan-snapshot tests, because only dbe-tool can be run here.
notes: This repeats an earlier run's result (q19 -53% then, -46..-48% now). A follow-up could check whether DistributivityRule's factoring should keep the derived filters for nested ORs below an AND root; currently the rule only fires on a root OR.

title: Length-aware selectivity for contains()/LIKE scan filters v2
summary: I added a TableFilterType::EXPRESSION_FILTER case to RelationStatisticsHelper::InspectTableFilter in relation_statistics_helper.cpp. It applies when the filter is a positive match function (contains, ~~ (LIKE), like_escape, prefix or suffix) whose first argument is not foldable and whose second argument is a non-NULL VARCHAR constant. Let L be the literal length with %/_ excluded for LIKE, capped at 64. The selectivity is then max(0.2*0.75^L, 0.01) and the estimate is max(1, card*sel). Any other expression filter keeps the old behavior (the flat 0.2 default). The helper is a file-static function, so no header changed. The build is OK. Full bench: q09 went from 1227 to 763ms (-37.8%) and the geomean improved by 3.6%. Every other template was within noise. q04 showed +7.4% in the first run, but it has no LIKE, and a rerun gave -11.6%. A rerun of q09 gave 1200 to 770ms (-35.9%). Results checks passed in bench. I did not run `profile q09.m0`, so the join-order flip is inferred from the timing and not confirmed in a plan.
notes: This is the same mechanism as the earlier contains-selectivity run, and the q09 gain reproduced (-36..-38%). An earlier note said lineitem lost its bloom filter after the join-order flip; it still nets a large win. A possible follow-up is an ILIKE / regexp_matches literal-length estimate, but no visible query uses them.

title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins v2 (all 3 gates)
summary:
Perfect hash join now covers RIGHT joins, with all three gates fixed.
- Optimizer: join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp now computes min/max aggregates for RIGHT joins too (single integral equality condition), not just INNER.
- CanDoPerfectHashJoin: accepts JoinType::RIGHT; guards NULL min/max (happens when every build key is NULL); dup check is now `ht.Count() > build_range + 1`, so fully dense key sets qualify.
- Range cap: MAX_BUILD_SIZE (1M) stays for all joins. Joins that keep unmatched build rows (RIGHT) may go up to 4M, but only if the build fills at least half the range. I went beyond the plan here: q13's key range is 1.5M, so with the cap untouched the fast path never fires.
- Build fill: skips NULL keys. RIGHT joins keep those rows in the HT with has_null=false. They never match, so the outer scan emits them as unmatched.
- Match tracking: the probe sets a per-slot byte array. The build keeps the slot→HT-row mapping (addresses plus selection vectors). New PerfectHashJoinExecutor::FlushFoundMatch() writes found_match into the HT rows. It runs in HashJoinGlobalSourceState::Initialize, before the existing SCAN_HT outer scan, which is unchanged.

Measured (bench, against current best):
- q13: -20.0%, -17.9%, -18.0%, -18.2% (780→638ms).
- Final full run: geomean -2.5%. q05 -14% and q07 -5% are likely noise. q03 +4.6%, q04 +3.7% and q09 +3.7% are inside the ~5% noise band, and those plans don't touch the changed paths much.
- First version allowed the 4M range for INNER joins too: q14 +52%, q18 +13..16%, geomean +2.7%. Limiting the large range to RIGHT joins fixed it (q14 -1.3%, q18 +0.9%).
- q08 swung between +12% and -3.4% across reruns, which is noise.

Correctness checks (via `dbe-tool sql`): integer keys (perfect path) gave the same results as VARCHAR keys (regular hash join) for:
- RIGHT join with NULL build keys and unmatched build rows
- RIGHT join with duplicate build keys (falls back to the regular join)
- RIGHT join with a 2M dense build range
- dense INNER join
notes:
- The perfect hash table is built serially in Finalize, and choosing it turns off the probe-side Bloom filter (CanUseBloomFilter gets is_perfect_hashtable=true). So for dimensions of 1.5–2M keys with small or medium probes it loses to the parallel regular build: q14 lineitem-part (+52%) and q18 customer-orders (+13%) when the large range was allowed for INNER.
- That is why ranges over 1M are limited to RIGHT joins. A small-probe RIGHT join on a 1–4M dense dimension could still pay the serial build, possibly a small regression. A cardinality-based gate would be safer.
- Follow-up: parallelize the perfect build (FullScanHashTable gather) or keep the BF alongside it. That could unlock large-range perfect HJ for INNER joins.
- found_match flush is serial over the build rows in source Initialize: about 1.5M sequential writes, cheap.
- I changed one header (perfect_hash_join_executor.hpp, private members plus one method). Only the join operator files include it, so the rebuild was quick.

title: Substring prefilter over contiguous string runs for LIKE/contains scan filters
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q13 -7.7%; needs at least -13.8%)
summary:
I added a substring prefilter to `ColumnData::Filter` in `src/storage/table/column_data.cpp`; it is the only file changed. It builds, and q13 and q09 got faster in every bench run.

**What it does.** It applies when the filter is a top-level EXPRESSION_FILTER of the form `~~`, `!~~` or `contains`, possibly wrapped in one or more NOTs. The column must be a direct column reference of type VARCHAR, the pattern a non-NULL VARCHAR constant, and the result a FLAT vector of at most STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE rows. For LIKE patterns it only applies when the wildcards are all `%` (no `_` or `\`); it then takes the longest literal segment. For contains it uses the whole needle. The literal must be at least 2 bytes.

For each row in the incoming selection:
- **NULL rows** are dropped.
- **Inlined strings (12 bytes or less)** become candidates for the normal path.
- **Longer strings** are grouped into runs where each string's data starts exactly where the previous one ends. Each run is searched once with SSE2: compare the first and last byte, then `memcmp` to confirm. The final block overlaps the previous one instead of falling back to a scalar tail. A short scalar loop covers runs too small for one block and builds without SSE2.

A hit counts only if it lies entirely inside one string. That string becomes a candidate, and the search resumes at the end of that string.

Only candidates go through the original `ColumnSegment::FilterSelection`, with a smaller selection. Rows without the literal are decided directly: false for positive LIKE/contains, true for negated ones. NULLs are always excluded, and the original row order is kept. The new selection is installed with `sel.Initialize`, so the incoming selection is never written to.

**Correctness checks** (row counts or hash sums, compared with the same filter on `s||''`, which is not pushed down):
- On orders: NOT LIKE '%unusual%packages%', LIKE, contains, NOT contains, NOT LIKE '%s. %'. All equal.
- On a temp table with NULLs, inlined and long strings, prefix patterns, and a needle longer than any string: all differences were 0.

**Bench against the current best:**

| Run | q13 | q09 | Other templates |
|---|---|---|---|
| q13 + q09 only | 689.6 → 605.5 ms (-12.2%) | 773.2 → 729.1 ms (-5.7%) | – |
| Full bench | -6.5% | -8.0% | all within noise except q08 +11.9% |
| q08 + q13 rerun | -8.3% | – | q08 +0.4% |

The full-bench geomean was -0.8%. q08 has no LIKE filter, so the +11.9% looks like noise; the rerun supports that.
notes:
- **Testing pitfall:** to check NOT LIKE against a filter that blocks pushdown, use `s||''`, not `concat(s,'')`. `concat` turns NULL into `''`, so counts differ by exactly the number of NULLs and look like a bug.
- **Re-parsing:** the filter expression is re-parsed for every vector. It is cheap, but the result could be cached in the filter state, at the cost of a header change.
- **Follow-ups:**
  - Run the full multi-segment LIKE match (each segment in order) inside the run, so candidates never go through the generic matcher.
  - Choose the rarest segment as the needle rather than the longest.
  - Extend the prefilter to filters inside CONJUNCTION_AND.
  - Add a NEON path for ARM.

title: Bloom filter on first key of multi-key hash joins
summary:
Hash joins with more than one equality key can now get a Bloom filter (BF) on their first key; before, they got none. Measured q09 at -18..-22% across four bench runs (best run 767.9→594.8ms). Last full bench: geomean -3.0%. Other templates moved within ±8% between runs, which is noise.

Changes:
- `src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp`: `CanUseBloomFilter` no longer requires `conditions.size()==1`. In `FinalizeFilters`, the BF is only considered for the filter where `join_condition[filter_idx]==0`. `PushBloomFilter` already uses condition 0's key name, type and null handling.
- `src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp`: the hash table's own hash combines all equality keys, so it doesn't match what the probe side computes for a single column. When the BF is set up and there is more than one equality key, `Finalize` now gathers key column 0 from the row locations (new static helper `InsertFirstKeyIntoBloomFilter`), hashes it alone with `VectorOperations::Hash` (the same call `BFTableFilter` uses on the probe side) and inserts that into the BF. `InsertHashes` only inserts the combined hash into the BF for single-key joins. The single-key path is unchanged.

Correctness spot-checks: a two-int-key join gave the same count with and without pushdown (pushdown blocked with `col+0` keys): 295319. A NULL-able first key with IS NOT DISTINCT FROM also matched: 196595 both ways. A VARCHAR first key and a join mixing equality and non-equality conditions both ran without errors. Bench result checks passed on all visible templates.
notes:
q04 sometimes showed +7..+15% in bench runs. I don't think the change causes it:
- q04 has only single-key joins, so the new code never runs for it.
- It stayed at +15% with the feature fully disabled (the `size()==1` gate restored).
- Run alone it came out -6.3%, and in the final full bench -2.3%.

It looks like noise that depends on run order, or code layout in `join_hashtable.cpp`, where the hot probe loops live. Moving the BF code out of `InsertHashes` into `Finalize` (the shipped version) did not change it.

Follow-up idea: build the BF on whichever equality key is most selective instead of always key 0, or push one BF per key, each with its own single-column hash.

title: Join key-set range filter through compress projections
summary:
I made two changes:

1. **Join filters now pass through integral-compression projections.** `PushdownJoinFilterExpression` in `join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp` now follows `__internal_compress_integral_*(x, const_offset)` down to the column and records the offset in a new `JoinFilterPushdownColumn::storage_offset` field (a `Value`; NULL means no offset).
   - The UNION rewrite copies the offset to the rewritten columns.
   - TopN and RowGroupPruner reject targets that carry an offset.
   - Offsets that are UHUGEINT, NULL or non-integral are rejected, and so are nested offsets.

2. **Offset-aware filter values and a new range-set filter** in `physical_hash_join.cpp`.
   - A new helper `JoinFilterValueToStorage` adds the offset using HUGEINT arithmetic with an overflow check, then casts to the storage type. The min/max filters and the IN-list filter both use it.
   - The bloom filter is never pushed for offset columns.
   - New `PushRangeSetFilter`: for equality joins where `dynamic_or_filter_threshold < HT count <= 64*threshold` and the storage type is an integer of 64 bits or less, it scans the build keys, skips NULLs, sorts and dedups them, and splits them at the `4*threshold - 1` largest gaps. It then pushes an `OptionalFilter` holding an OR of those ranges (exact matches for single keys), so it is used for zonemap pruning only.

Measured with `dbe-tool bench` against the current best:
- **q18:** -8.9%, -7.8%, -5.9% and -7.9% across four runs (best 696–754 ms → yours 639–695 ms).
- **Rows scanned in the q18 profile:** lineitem 59,986,052 → 12,130,926 (17.5M with 50 ranges); orders 15M → 9.0M (that figure is from the 50-range run; I didn't capture it for the final 200-range build).
- **q04:** -14% in one run and +8% in another. That's noise; its plan doesn't change in any way that matters.
- **q17:** +4–5.6% in three runs and +0.4% when rerun alone. It does get the range filter (2001 random partkeys, nothing pruned), but these filters are checked only once per row group or segment, never per row, so I believe it is noise.
- **Geomean** across all templates: -0.8% and -0.4% in the two full runs.

Correctness spot checks via `dbe-tool sql` gave identical results for a semi join with 600 keys, an inner join with 400 keys (plain columns), and a HAVING semi join over compressed keys with 2149 keys, each compared against an equivalent query that doesn't use the join filter.
notes:
- `OptionalFilter` is evaluated only in `RowGroup::CheckZonemap` (once per row group) and in `CheckZonemapSegments` (once per segment, because `segment_checked` is set). So many ranges are cheap; going from 50 to 200 ranges cut lineitem rows from 17.5M to 12.1M.
- One range per key (up to 64×threshold) would prune slightly more. I didn't try it because the range checks compare `Value` objects, which is slow.
- The remaining q18 time is mostly the 15M-group aggregate in the subquery (5.1s CPU) and the customer join.
- Follow-up idea: push the bloom filter through the compression offset (hash `x - offset` masked to the key width; an earlier run measured q09 -8% that way). It's left out here to keep this change to one idea.
- The header change in `join_filter_pushdown.hpp` rebuilt quickly.

title: Exact key-bitmap mode for join Bloom filter on dense integer build keys
summary:
I added an exact key-bitmap mode to the join Bloom filter for dense integer build keys. It speeds up four visible templates: q03 -16 to -20%, q04 -19 to -21%, q09 -12 to -13%, q16 -5 to -8%. Full-bench geomean is -4.4%, with nothing slower outside noise (q05 was +3.6%, then -1.6% on rerun).

Changes:
- **BloomFilter (bloom_filter.hpp/.cpp).** New `SetExactRange(min, range)`. In this mode `Initialize` allocates range/64+1 words instead of hashed sectors. Keys are widened to 64 bits (signed values sign-extended, unsigned zero-extended) and stored as the offset key - min. Values outside the range miss. Inserts use an atomic `fetch_or` because the finalize step runs in parallel.
- **Probe (`BFTableFilter::Filter`).** The exact path skips hashing. It uses `UnifiedVectorFormat`: flat vectors are indexed through `sel` directly, other vector types (sequence, dictionary, constant) are sliced first when `sel` is set. NULL keys miss.
- **`FilterValue` and `CheckStatistics`** handle exact mode. Statistics pruning compares range overlap and, for ranges up to 2048, probes each value. It never returns ALWAYS_FALSE when NULLs pass the filter. If the key type doesn't match, or an out-of-range key was ever inserted (an overflow flag), the filter lets everything through.
- **Gate (`TrySetExactBloomFilter` in physical_hash_join.cpp).** It runs at the existing point where the Bloom filter is chosen, so it already requires no cast, no storage offset, key 0, an equality and a hash table that isn't perfect. It also requires: NULLs not equal, left type == right type == HT key type, an 8..64-bit integer key, and range < min(2^32, 128*ht.Count()).
- **Fill (`JoinHashTable::Finalize`).** In exact mode it gathers key column 0 and sets bits, replacing both the single-key hash insert and the first-key hash insert for multi-key joins.

Correctness: on TEMP tables, results matched `SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown'` for INT, TINYINT, SMALLINT, UINTEGER, UBIGINT and BIGINT keys. The tests included negative keys, keys at both min/max boundaries, NULLs on both sides, IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, multi-key, RIGHT and semi joins. EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed the probe scan returning exactly as many rows as the join (300,004), so exact mode was active.
notes: The biggest gains on this base are q03 and q04, which earlier runs did not measure, plus q09 and q16. q21 is not in the visible set here. Testing tip: the selectivity wrapper switches the filter off when about 30% of probe rows pass, so use a sparse build side (about 10%) to see exact row counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE. One surprise: a SMALLINT cast-overflow query raised a conversion error only with join_filter_pushdown disabled, not with it enabled. It looks like a plan-ordering difference unrelated to this change; I didn't check it against the current best. Possible follow-ups: allow it for IS NOT DISTINCT FROM by recording whether a NULL was inserted, and allow probe columns with a storage offset by shifting the bitmap minimum.

title: Exact bitmap BF through CM compress offset
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q09 -3.9%; needs at least -8.6%)
visible geomean got slower (+0.5%)
summary:
Join filters can now push the exact-bitmap Bloom filter through compressed-materialization integral compression (__internal_compress_integral_*(x, off)). Before this, only shifted min/max and range-set filters went through; the BF was skipped.
- bloom_filter.hpp/.cpp: BFTableFilter gets has_key_offset/key_offset (SetKeyOffset), carried over in Copy. In exact mode the probe looks up widen(scanned value) - key_offset, with 64-bit wrapping. Widening is sign-extend for signed and zero-extend for unsigned storage types. The same shift is applied in Filter, FilterValue and CheckStatistics. CheckStatistics uses a separate offset version: it maps [min,max] to a contiguous arc of bitmap positions and prunes only if the arc doesn't wrap and lies entirely past the bitmap range; otherwise it probes each value when the range is ≤2048. If a filter has an offset but isn't exact, it lets every row pass.
- physical_hash_join.cpp: FinalizeFilters has a new branch. It applies when storage_offset is set, the filter is on join key 0, CanUseBloomFilter holds, and the offset converts to 64 bits (TryGetExactKeyOffset; storage type must be an integer of 64 bits or less). In that case it runs the exact gate on the raw compressed-key min/max before Finalize fills the bitmap. Only if that makes the filter exact does it turn on the BF build and defer the push. PushBloomFilter finds the probe column for key 0; if it has an offset, it pushes only when the filter is exact and has no overflow, using the storage type as key_type and setting key_offset. A hashed BF is never pushed through an offset.
Measured: q09 orders scan went from 15M to 2.94M rows. Bench q09 -9.2% / -9.0% (534→485, 514→468 ms). Full-suite geomean -0.3%. q04 showed +7.4% in the first run and -6.8% when rerun (noise); everything else within noise.
Correctness: TEMP tables with a 30M-row probe (with NULL keys) and a 15M-row build filtered to 10%, where CM compresses both join sides. Tested BIGINT keys starting at 1e9 (offset 1e9), negative BIGINT keys (−1e12−i), UBIGINT keys starting at 3e9, and a RIGHT join. All results equal those with SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown'. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows probe scans dropping from 30M to 3M rows for the positive and negative BIGINT cases; the UBIGINT and RIGHT-join scan counts were not checked.
notes: The exact gate must use the raw (compressed) min/max from final_min_max. min_val/max_val in FinalizeFilters have already been converted to storage values with the offset added. In my tests CM compressed only BIGINT/UBIGINT keys; INTEGER keys weren't compressed, so the offset path didn't run for them. To get CM on a join in temp-table tests you need a build of about 15M rows. q09 orders HJ CPU remains roughly build-side bound (3.27M inserts). Serialization of key_offset was not added: BF deserialization already creates a detached filter. Possible follow-up: q05/q07/q08 didn't move measurably, so CM-under-join with a dense key is mostly a q09 pattern in this workload.

title: Large perfect hash aggregate (up to 22 bits) with parallel combine and source
reasons: q16 slower by 14.3% (26 ms), beyond its 7.9% threshold
q18 slower by 7.8% (48 ms), beyond its 5.0% threshold
notes:
- The per-thread cost of a large perfect hash aggregate scales with threads × slots touched, not with rows. A wrong input estimate therefore hurts a lot: q17's estimate came from a join against a DELIM_SCAN (estimated at 1.08M rows, actually 2,001), which inflated the aggregate input estimate to 34.7M.
- Lazy per-slot state initialization was necessary, and it also sped up q13 further. Even with it, a sparse input costs about one page fault per first touch of a slot (q17 still had +16% before the DELIM_SCAN guard).
- There is no jemalloc in this build, so the big tables are fresh mmap allocations every query.
- Inputs with estimates that are too high but no DELIM_SCAN (for example, joins with very selective filters the estimator misses) could still be slowed down by this path. A follow-up could be a runtime fallback that delays allocating a thread's local table until it has seen enough rows.
- To see the full profile (the tree output gets truncated): PRAGMA enable_profiling='json'; SET profiling_output=...; then extract "operator_name", "operator_timing" and "Estimated Cardinality" with regexp_extract_all over read_text.

title: Distinct HT partitioned on group hash
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q16 -7.4%; needs at least -7.9%)
summary:
I fixed both review points; the tree builds. The q16 gain is real but noisy: -10.9%, -9.8%, -3.3% and +0.2% across four runs.

What changed since the rejected version:

1. **Only the top 4 radix bits come from the group hash.** The distinct hash table now takes bits [44,48) from hash(main groups) instead of all 12. The lower radix bits still come from the full hash(G,x), so repartitioning can still split a heavy group. The stored hash is used consistently, so correctness is unchanged.
2. **New runtime memory gate.** `RadixPartitionedHashTable::EnablePartitionPrefix(GlobalSinkState&, idx_t)` is called from the `HashAggregateGlobalSinkState` constructor with the child's row estimate. Prefix mode turns on only when estimated rows × (row width + 16) ≤ query memory limit / 16. The existing plan-time setup is kept: grouped aggregates with estimated output ≥ 4096 that have distinct tables. Ungrouped DISTINCT never turns it on.

**Spill check with one dominant group** (90% of rows in one group, 40M distinct x, about 5000 groups, 8 threads, `memory_limit=500MB`):
- Baseline (feature disabled): 6.42 s.
- Previous 12-bit version: failed with Out of Memory.
- 4-bit version without the gate: OOM. A 2-bit version without the gate passed but took 10.5–11.3 s (+65%), which is what led to the gate.
- Final version: 6.55 s, because the gate turns the feature off. Results match.

**In-memory checks, no memory limit:**
- 4M rows with 90% in the NULL group: 498–543 ms baseline vs 543–573 ms mine, about +7%. This is the remaining cost on an adversarial case.
- 8M rows spread evenly over 5000 groups: 904 ms baseline vs 801 ms mine, -11%.

**q16:** the best version measured between 174 and 195 ms; mine measured 164–182 ms.

**Full bench:** geomean -0.1%. Nothing outside ±5%: q18 and q19 were +4.3%, q02 -4.1%.
notes:
- The q16 gain is very noisy on this tree: my build is steady at 164–182 ms, while the best version swings between 174 and 195 ms. Per run: -10.9, -3.3, -9.8, +0.2%.
- Taking all 12 radix bits from the group hash makes a dominant group OOM under a low memory limit. Even 2 bits without a memory gate was 65% slower in the spill case.
- I could not run the baseline binary directly. Baseline numbers came from rebuilding with the plan gate forced off (`if (false && ...)`), which gives the original code path; that change is reverted in the final tree.
- Possible follow-up: choose the number of prefix bits from the final radix bits, or measure skew from HLL or a partition histogram before combining. Either would need a global decision before any rows are sunk, because all threads must hash the same way.

title: Semi-join RHS-aware estimate + HAVING selectivity
summary:
I changed one function in `src/optimizer/join_order/cardinality_estimator.cpp`: `CalculateUpdatedDenom`, which estimates how many rows a join returns. For SEMI joins it used to assume the left side shrinks by a fixed factor of 5, whatever the right side's size. Now the factor is max(5, tdom / rhs_cardinality), where tdom is the join key's distinct-count estimate and rhs_cardinality is the right side's estimated row count (its numerator over its denominator). The check is skipped if tdom is 0 or the right side is estimated below 1 row. ANTI joins are unchanged, because a small right side means an anti join removes fewer rows, not more.

I did not make the planned change to `relation_manager.cpp` because it isn't needed in this tree. The HAVING filter already gets the 0.2 selectivity, since a filter directly above an aggregate is treated as a data-source filter: in EXPLAIN the subquery estimate drops from ~5.36M to ~1.07M after the HAVING. Adding another 0.2 would have counted it twice.

Plan effect on q18.m0 (seen in EXPLAIN ANALYZE): the orders ⋈ IN-subquery estimate drops from ~3M to ~1M rows, which is now below customer's 1.5M. Customer becomes the probe side and the 111-row side becomes the build side. That hash join went from 0.52s to 0.01s, and profiled total time from 0.956s to 0.869s. The customer scan still reads ~1.49M rows; the dynamic filter on it prunes very little.

Bench (my build vs current best):
- **First full run:** q18 -9.3%, q16 -6.6%, q04 -5.7%, q17 +6.8%, everything else within ±5%, geomean -2.3%.
- **Rerun of q04/q16/q17/q18:** q18 -6.1%, q04 -1.9%, q16 +2.6%, q17 +0.9%, geomean -1.2%.

So the q17 jump was noise (its plan has no SEMI join), and so were the q04 and q16 gains. The real effect is q18 at -6 to -9%. The tree builds and the bench result checks passed.
notes:
- **Planned second change dropped:** the issue's HAVING 0.2 in `relation_manager.cpp` is already there in this tree (`datasource_filters` holds the HAVING filter because its child is an aggregate), so I didn't add it. A memory from an earlier run said both pieces were needed; on the current tree only the SEMI denominator change is.
- **The bound assumes a duplicate-free right side:** tdom/rhs is the best case. If the right side has many duplicate keys, the semi join is over-estimated as selective, but never below lhs/tdom.
- **Follow-up:** after the flip, q18's customer scan still reads ~1.49M rows (about 0.19s CPU) even though the join only needs 111 customer keys. The dynamic OR-of-equalities filter on that scan prunes little because those keys are spread across the table. A bitmap Bloom filter at that scan might save the rest.

title: OR-of-ranges scan filter as dense-mask ExpressionFilter
summary:
I added a fast path for EXPRESSION_FILTER in ColumnSegment::FilterSelection (src/storage/table/column_segment.cpp; the change is in this one file). When the expression is an AND/OR tree whose leaves are BETWEENs or comparisons (=, !=, <, <=, >, >=) of the filtered column (BOUND_REF 0, exact type) against non-NULL constants of the same type, the selected values are first gathered into a dense array. Each node is then evaluated as a branch-free uint8 mask and ANDed/ORed together. The mask is ANDed with validity and turned into a fresh selection vector. Anything else falls back to the existing ExpressionExecutor path unchanged.

Measured: the lineitem scan in the q19.m0 profile went from 5.12s to 4.76s CPU, and total time from 0.725s to 0.670s. `bench q19` gave -9.0%, -7.5% and -11.1% in three runs; the full bench had q19 at only -2.9% because that run was noisy. The full bench geomean was -0.1%. That run showed q08 +12.5% and q17 +9.9%, but a re-run gave +0.6% and -0.2%, and q22 went from +6.3% to -1.1%. I didn't trace the plans of those templates to rule out the new path, but the re-runs say it was noise.

Correctness check: on a temp table with NULLs (DECIMAL, INTEGER, DATE, UTINYINT columns), 4 count queries matched the same predicates rewritten with casts so they fall back to the generic path. title: Large perfect HA v2: large-mode-only code paths, plan-identical guard for other templates
reasons: q18 slower by 8.7% (50 ms), beyond its 5.0% threshold
summary:

The plan and q18's own inner agg (~500 ms in both modes) are identical, so this looks like a bench-process artifact. Expect the official bench to flag q18 again.

title: FSST batched decode + substring prefilter bundle (q13)
summary:
Combined two changes for scans of FSST string columns. q13 measured -15.1%, -15.3% and -15.8% across three bench runs, with one outlier at -3.4%; all other templates were within noise.

1) src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp: a new FSSTScanState::DecompressStrings, used by both StringScanPartial (flat decode) and Select.
- It decodes each vector's strings back to back into shared heap allocations. Each allocation holds up to 64KB of worst-case output (8 bytes per compressed byte), plus 32 bytes of slack.
- Each string's write bound is the space left in the allocation, which always covers the worst case of the strings still to come.
- Strings that fit inline (12 bytes or less) are copied into their string_t, so their bytes are not kept in the heap. The allocation is shrunk to the bytes actually used.
- Decoding no longer goes through duckdb_fsst_decompress. It uses a simple loop that handles one code per iteration: copy the 8-byte symbol, add len[code], and copy the literal byte after an escape. This is safe because the symbol-table import always sets len to 1..8. An escape as the last byte throws a corrupt-file error.
- The all-values-inlined case keeps the old per-string path.

2) src/storage/table/column_segment.cpp: a substring prefilter for ExpressionFilter.
- It applies to LIKE (`~~`), NOT LIKE (`!~~`) and contains, optionally wrapped in NOT. The first argument must be the column itself (VARCHAR) and the second a non-NULL VARCHAR constant.
- The needle is the longest literal between '%'/'_' wildcards, or the whole contains argument, and must be at least 2 bytes.
- Strings stored back to back in memory are grouped into runs. Each run is searched once with an SSE2 first-byte/last-byte scan (overlapping final block, scalar fallback), and each hit is mapped to its row. Hits that cross a row boundary are rejected.
- Only rows that contain the needle are passed to the original expression. In the negated case, non-NULL rows without the needle pass directly. NULL rows always fail.
- A fresh SelectionVector is always built. Anything that does not match these conditions falls back to the existing path.

Measurements (CPU time from EXPLAIN ANALYZE; hot wall times from repeated runs):
- Scanning lineitem with `l_comment <> 'x'`: 6.88s → 4.06s CPU; hot wall time is about 278ms now (no hot timing of the old build).
- The orders NOT LIKE scan costs 2.12s CPU against 1.98s for a trivial `<>` filter on the same column, so the LIKE evaluation itself is now nearly free.
- Full bench runs: the geomean came out -1.7% and +1.0%. Templates that looked slower once (q08 +7.5%, q16 +9.7%, q22 +6.7%) came back to noise when rerun (q08 -3.6%, q16 +1.2%).
- The bench showed results correct on every visible template.
- Extra checks:
  - sum(hash(col)) on l_comment, o_comment and p_name was identical between the new decode path and the original one (reached with enable_fsst_vectors=true).
  - NOT LIKE, LIKE, NOT contains, contains and a LIKE pattern with '_' gave the same counts as the same filter on `col||''` (which is not pushed into the scan), on both the orders data and a temp table with NULLs, inlined strings and needles split across rows.
notes:
- The key finding: FSST scan cost was about 100ns per string almost regardless of length (27-byte strings 115ns/row, 48-byte strings 133ns/row), so it is per-string overhead, not per-byte work. The 4-code fast loop and tail branches of duckdb_fsst_decompress cost more than the decode itself.
- Follow-up idea: apply the same simple decode loop to FSSTVector::DecompressVector (src/common/types/vector.cpp) and to dict_fsst decompression. Both still call duckdb_fsst_decompress per string.
- Bench noise on this machine is about ±8% per template in a single run. Rerun before trusting a regression.
- The q13 scan now spends about 1.9s CPU on decode-plus-scan and almost nothing on the LIKE itself. The next q13 target is the perfect hash group-by (about 1.0s CPU) or skipping decode entirely, e.g. by searching compressed codes.

title: Bloom filter for hash joins whose build side is a DELIM_GET
reasons: q14 slower by 8.0% (12 ms), beyond its 5.1% threshold
summary:
I changed one line in src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp. When a hash join's build side is a LOGICAL_DELIM_GET, build_side_has_filter is now true. Before, it was set by IsFiltering(join.children[0]), which tests the probe side, so a bare probe-side scan never got a Bloom filter. The runtime gates in CanUseBloomFilter still apply: the comparison must be COMPARE_EQUAL, the hash table must not be perfect, and the probe estimate must be larger than the build count. The selectivity check that switches off an unselective filter also still applies. The join-type gating in GenerateJoinFilters (no MARK/SINGLE/LEFT/OUTER/ANTI) is unchanged.

Measured on q22: the orders scan in the decorrelated NOT EXISTS now has `o_custkey IN BF(c_custkey)` and emits 1.9M rows instead of 15M. Bench gave q22 -23.6%, -26.7%, -19.8% and -18.9% over four runs. Results matched in every bench run.

q17, the target in the issue, did not improve: +1.0%, -4.3%, +18.7%, -1.3%, which is noise. I did not check why. My guess is that its DELIM-build join uses a perfect hash table, which CanUseBloomFilter refuses on purpose. q02 and q04 went both ways between runs (q02 -16%, +7%, +22%, -1%), so they are noise. The machine was very noisy: q03, which has no DELIM join, read +25% and +31% in two runs and -4% in a third. Geomean was -0.1% on the full run, +12% on a noisy subset and -6.6% on the last subset.
notes: The issue predicted a q17 gain, but none showed up. Its subquery join (lineitem against the DELIM_GET of about 2K part keys) probably uses a perfect or sparse-perfect hash table, and CanUseBloomFilter returns false when is_perfect_hashtable is set. A follow-up could allow the exact-bitmap BF for perfect hash tables when the min/max range is sparse compared with the build count, but earlier memory notes ([[bf-sparse-perfect-hj-no-gain]]) found that unhelpful on q21. Benchmark noise was extreme (±30% on untouched templates), so re-run subsets before trusting any single run.

title: Rerun: BF for hash joins whose build side is a DELIM_GET
summary: I reapplied the E0015 one-line change. Before, it ran IsFiltering on the probe side (children[0]), so a join whose build side is a DELIM_GET never got a Bloom filter. All other cases still use the existing IsFiltering check, and the runtime gates (CanUseBloomFilter, the selectivity auto-disable) are untouched. The build passed. title: Stop compressing hash-join keys in compressed materialization
reasons: visible geomean got slower (+0.6%)
summary:
In CompressedMaterialization::CompressComparisonJoin (src/optimizer/compressed_materialization/compress_comparison_join.cpp), I removed the block that compressed both columns of a single equality condition generically and added the probe key to probe_compress_bindings. Every condition now goes through GetReferencedBindings, so join keys are never compressed. Build-side payload columns are still compressed, and aggregate/order/distinct CM is unchanged.

Why it was slow: the hash join only builds a Bloom filter when `storage_offset.IsNull()` (physical_hash_join.cpp:1059). A probe key under a CM compress projection gets an offset, so its probe scan only got min/max filters and never the BF. With the change, q09's orders scan and q03's lineitem scan get the BF, as the profiles show.

Bench (4 runs, the bench itself is ±10-20% noisy): q09 -7.1%, -11.9%, -14.3%, -15.3%, -19.0%. q03 swung between +9.6% and -17% (-11.6% on the last full run). Last full bench geomean -4.8%, with nothing slower than +4.6% (q04).

The q19 "+21%" from early runs was noise. The q19 plan is identical with and without the change because CM never touches that join, and an unchanged tree measured -17% on q19. q13 still uses the perfect RIGHT HJ (0.39s for 15M probe rows) and measured -5.9..+3.9%. q18 was ±1.6%. I didn't try variant B (no join CM at all) because the key-only variant already gives the expected q09/q03 gains.
notes:
The bench is very noisy, ±20% per template on identical code (q19 and q08 especially), so compare profile plans before believing a regression.

On q13 the aggregate CM now adds a 15M-row compress projection (about 0.58s CPU) above the RIGHT join, replacing the old decompress/compress pair. Follow-up idea: skip the aggregate CM compress when the group key comes straight from a large join output and the perfect HA already uses the stats range.

An alternative fix would have been to let BF push through the storage_offset by shifting keys on the probe side. Removing key compression is simpler and also drops the projections.

visible geomean got slower (+0.0%)

title: Exact-bitmap BF pushed through CM compress offset
reasons: visible geomean got slower (+0.0%)
summary:
Hash joins now push their exact-bitmap Bloom filter to the probe scan even when compressed materialization has stored the join key as value − offset. Before this change that case got only min/max filters. Build OK. Over three bench runs q09 was −12.9%, −10.2% and −11.1% (about 500 → 450 ms). On the full bench nothing else moved more than ±10%, and the bench treats differences under ~5% as noise. The geomean was −1.9% on the full bench and −2.1% / −4.5% on the subset runs.

What changed:
1) bloom_filter.hpp/.cpp: BFTableFilter has a new `key_offset` field (default 0) with SetKeyOffset. Copy and Serialize/Deserialize carry it (property 203, with a default). The exact-mode Filter, FilterValue and CheckStatistics paths subtract key_offset from the sign- or zero-extended 64-bit storage value before the bitmap test. The subtraction is modulo 2^64. A real member always maps exactly to its stored key, and wraparound can only cause a false positive, which the join then discards. CheckStatisticsExact now checks that the shifted key range round-trips into the column type and is ordered; if not, it returns NO_PRUNING_POSSIBLE. This avoids wrong row-group pruning when the range can't be represented in that type.
2) physical_hash_join.cpp FinalizeFilters has a new branch. It fires when storage_offset is non-null, the condition type is integral, the filter is on join condition 0 and CanUseBloomFilter passes. It calls TrySetExactBloomFilter with the RAW min/max from the hash table (before the offset is applied), and defers the push only if the filter really is exact. A hashed filter is never pushed through an offset. PushBloomFilter sets key_type to the probe column's storage type and sets key_offset from the offset's low 64 bits (via HUGEINT). If the filter is not exact it pushes nothing.

Correctness checks: I compared each query against SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown', and the results matched in both tests.
- 15M-row BIGINT build with keys starting at 1e12 (offset 1e12) against a 60M-row probe starting below the offset. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the filter taking the probe from 45M rows (after the min/max range filter) to 6.4M.
- Negative INTEGER keys (around −2e9) with NULLs on both sides, as an inner join and as an IN subquery.
notes: q04 does not reach this path: its lineitem probe already gets an exact filter without compression in the current best plan. The q04 −7..−9% and +8.8% seen across runs, and q03's −5.5%/+9.2%, are noise, so the issue's expected q04 gain is not real on this tree. The only real gain is q09. The modular subtraction of the offset needs no HUGEINT on the probe path, because wraparound only produces false positives. However, the stats-pruning range check needs the round-trip check, since a cast inside the compression chain can make the shifted range unrepresentable in the probe type. CheckStatistics returning ALWAYS_TRUE on false positives is harmless.

summary:
I rebuilt both retired changes (E0019 and E0020) from their ledger descriptions, because their diffs were not in the tree. The tree builds. The Bloom filter now reaches the probe through the compression offset: in q04, the lineitem scan output drops from 37.9M rows to 2.29M (EXPLAIN ANALYZE). The plan is now a RIGHT_SEMI hash join with min/max and Bloom filter (BF) dynamic filters.

Bench (my build vs current best):
- q04: -26.2%, -34.6%, -28.1%, -29.3% (about 240 → 170 ms)
- q09: -10.8%, -13.2%, -12.8% (about 510 → 450 ms)
- Full-bench geomean: -2.6% and -3.8%

Changes:
1) deliminator.cpp: SelectionIsReplaceableByJoinFilter lets a SEMI delim join drop its DelimGet join even when the outer side has a selection. It applies only when:

CheckStatisticsExact first checks that the shifted key range round-trips into the column type and is ordered; otherwise it returns NO_PRUNING_POSSIBLE.
4) physical_hash_join.cpp FinalizeFilters: a new branch for an integral probe column with storage_offset, on condition 0, that passes CanUseBloomFilter. PushBloomFilter sets key_type to the probe storage type and key_offset to the offset's low 64 bits.

Correctness: every check matched SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown,deliminator':
- q04-style EXISTS with new dates
- NOT EXISTS
- IN over customer/orders
- EXISTS over a two-table join inside the subquery
- EXISTS whose correlation key is sometimes NULL
- generated data with NULLs on both sides (EXISTS, IN, NOT EXISTS, NOT IN)
- shifted keys (`l_orderkey + 3`, `o_orderkey - 100`, `o_orderkey * 2`) through the offset BF

The risk is q07. In 5 bench runs it was +12.4, +4.7, +8.2, +3.7 and +4.2%. The offset BF now also fires on q07's orders scan: an orderkey BF built from the lineitem join takes the scan from 15M rows to 100k, but a custkey BF had already cut it to 1.2M.

What I measured:

I could not explain why bench and direct timing disagree. If the judge flags q07, the next step is to look at how the scan's adaptive filter orders two BF-filtered columns, or to gate the offset BF when the probe scan already has another selective BF.

The E0019 helper conditions were rebuilt from the ledger description, since the original diff was not in the tree.

title: Exact BF bitmap for small absolute key ranges
summary: I changed one function, TrySetExactBloomFilter in src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp. I added EXACT_BF_SMALL_RANGE = 1<<22. The key range cap is now max(count*128, 1<<22), and EXACT_BF_MAX_RANGE still bounds it. So any integer join key whose range is under about 4M values gets an exact bitmap (at most 512KB), however few keys the build side has. Before this, a small selective build side was capped at 128 bits per key, so its filter stayed hashed and let many false positives through. I checked the bitmap code in planner/filter/bloom_filter.cpp: it makes one shared allocation and one fill, not one per thread. The build passed (BUILD OK). The full bench matched the current best's results and ran 10.2% faster on the geomean: q17 -36.8%, q19 -35.3%, q08 -19.5%, q02 -18.9%, q13 -8.1%. The worst change was q07 at +1.5%, which is noise. I did not run the JSON profile the plan asked for, so I have not directly confirmed the drop in lineitem scan rows on q17; the evidence is the bench timings. Correctness checks: a 3-key build over a 4,194,303 range with a negative key and keys at both ends returned the expected 3 rows and sum. A 43-key build over a range of about 4.19M, probed with 9M rows, matched the result with SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown'.
notes: The gains were larger than the issue predicted: q19 and q02 also moved to exact mode, not just q17 and q08. A possible follow-up is raising the small-range limit to 1<<24 (2MB) for larger datasets, where dimension key ranges grow with the scale factor. That would need a check of L2-miss cost when the probe hit rate is low.

title: Deliminate selective ANTI delim joins (NOT EXISTS) with simple RHS
summary: In src/optimizer/deliminator.cpp, the SelectionIsReplaceableByJoinFilter gate now accepts ANTI delim joins as well as SEMI ones. All other guards are unchanged: one DelimGet, one INNER/SEMI child join with only colref = colref conditions, and a SubqueryIsSimple RHS. Two comments were updated. With this change, a NOT EXISTS with a simple equality correlation and a filtered outer query becomes a plain RIGHT_ANTI hash join. The NDF condition is converted to =, so runtime min/max + BF filters reach the RHS scan. The q22 profile confirms that the DELIM_JOIN, the inner HJ with the delim keys and the DISTINCT are gone, and the orders scan still has min/max + BF dynamic filters. Bench: q22 150.3→106.9ms (-28.9%), then -21.5% and -23.1% on reruns. Full-run geomean -4.2%. The other templates have no NOT EXISTS and their changes are noise. q14 showed a one-off +30.3%, then +4.3% on rerun; its plan can't change.
notes:
NULL semantics checked:
- RIGHT_ANTI keeps NULL build keys, because PrepareKeys skips null filtering when PropagatesBuildSide is true. NULL-key LHS rows are therefore still emitted by the unmatched-build scan.
- Plain ANTI gets no join filters (GenerateJoinFilters skips ANTI), and a NULL probe key with = never matches, so the row is emitted.
- The IS NOT NULL filter on the RHS replacing column makes NDF→= exact.

Checked on temp tables with NULL keys on both sides, in both build orientations (small outer and large outer), plus a correlated `<>` extra predicate. Every result matched `SET disabled_optimizers='deliminator'`.

Possible follow-up: MARK delim joins (IN / EXISTS in disjunctions) could use the same treatment, but MARK NULL semantics differ and would need their own check.

title: Parallel perfect-HJ build + dense INNER builds up to 4M range
summary:
The perfect hash join build now runs in parallel for builds with at least 64k rows, and INNER joins with a key range up to 4M now qualify when the keys fill at least half the range.

What I changed:
1. **Parallel key pass.** PerfectHashJoinExecutor::BuildPerfectHashTable allocates the table, an atomic key bitmap and a slot→row address array. A new PerfectHashJoinBuildEvent, scheduled from PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize, runs tasks over ranges of 16 hash-table chunks. Each task reads the key column, sets the key's bit with an atomic `fetch_or`, flags a duplicate if the bit was already set, and records the row address for the slot.
2. **Decision in FinishEvent.** FinishBuild copies the atomic bitmap into bitmap_build_idx, sets the dense flag and prepares the payload validity masks.
   - The join filters (FinalizeFilters) are now created at this point, once the perfect-or-not decision is known. The min/max chunk is held in the sink until then.
   - If a duplicate key was found, the join falls back to the regular `sink.ScheduleFinalize(*pipeline, *this)`, the same way HashJoinRepartitionEvent already does.
   - Otherwise a second event gathers the payload over slot ranges of 131072 (a multiple of 64), so tasks never share a validity word.
3. **RIGHT joins.** FlushFoundMatch uses the slot→row array on the parallel path.
4. **CanDoPerfectHashJoin.** I dropped the `!PropagatesBuildSide(op.join_type) ||` term, so INNER joins now take the existing ≥50% density rule for ranges up to 4M.

Builds under 64k rows still take the unchanged serial path.

Measured: I timed the serial build on a 2M-key dense build with a VARCHAR payload. ScanKeyColumn took 43–50ms, the selection fill plus duplicate check about 35ms, and the payload gather only about 13ms. Parallelising only the gather, as the issue proposed, left q14 33–47% slower once INNER builds were allowed. That is why the key pass is parallel too.

Bench with the final version, against the current best:
- **q14:** −6.9%, −7.2%, −7.3% in three targeted runs, and −23.4% in one full-bench run. Another full-bench run showed q14 at +22.5%, but four reruns right after came back at −7% (138–144ms against a best of 147–181ms), so I treat that one as noise.
- **q13:** −2.9% to −7.5%.
- **Full bench:** geomean −3.3% in the second full run. Everything else stayed within ±5%, apart from q03 (+5.6% and +10.8% in two runs) and q02 (+6.5% once). As far as I can tell neither of those joins can take the perfect path, so I read them as noise.

Correctness: on the benchmark DB I compared each query against the same query with an extra `o_custkey+1 = b.k+1` condition, which forces the regular hash join. All results matched for:
- an INNER join on a 3M-key dense build with NULL and VARCHAR payloads;
- a RIGHT join on a build at 2/3 density with NULL keys and NULL VARCHAR payloads;
- an INNER join with a duplicate key, which exercises the fallback.
notes:
- Dead end: the issue assumed the payload gather was the serial cost. Timing showed it is only ~15% of the serial build; ScanKeyColumn and the per-row duplicate/selection fill were 80–90ms for 2M rows. Parallelising only the gather made q14 +33–47% slower once INNER builds up to 4M were allowed.
- The parallel build only works because FinalizeFilters is deferred to the build event's FinishEvent (`sink.perfect_filter_min_max`). Without that, builds that turn out to have duplicates would lose their bloom filter on the fallback.
- Benchmark noise: q14 swung between +22% and −23% across full-bench runs, while targeted reruns were a steady −7%.
- Follow-ups:
  - q13 (RIGHT perfect join on customer) may gain more; the found-match flush is still a serial pass over all slots and could be parallelised by slot range.
  - The probe-side scan still emits rows in range that match no key for 50–99% dense INNER builds. An exact bitmap filter could be pushed for perfect joins (the bitmap is already built), which could also cover q14's 2M dense build.

title: Exact BF bitmap up to 2^27 bits when 1024 bits/key allows
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q05 -18.2%; needs at least -20.3%)
visible geomean got slower (+0.5%)
summary: I added a middle tier to TrySetExactBloomFilter in physical_hash_join.cpp. A join filter can now use the exact bitmap when the key range is below min(2^27 bits, which is 16MB, and count×1024 bits). The existing 128 bits/key rule, the 2^22 small-range floor and the 2^32 max guard are unchanged. The multiplication only happens when count ≤ 2^17, so it can't overflow; above that the 2^27 cap applies directly. I also updated the comment about memory. Exact-bitmap building, probing and the CM offset path already handle ranges up to 2^32, so nothing else changed. Build OK and result checks passed. Bench against best across 3 runs: q05 -9.1%, -18.3%, -20.5%. q04 went -14.8%, +14.2%, +1.0%, and q09 went +11.0%, +1.7%, +2.0%; both swing both ways, so I read them as noise. The first full-suite run had a geomean of -1.8%, with q03 -6% and q16 -5% there. I did not profile q05, so I haven't confirmed directly that its lineitem filter is now exact or that scan CPU fell to about 0.48s. The consistent q05 gain fits the hypothesis.
notes: The only gain I saw consistently is q05. q04 and q09 swung between -15% and +14% across reruns, which is bench noise. Worth checking in the full timing run that q09 does not regress. Follow-up idea: a sparse two-level or blocked exact bitmap for ranges above 2^27.

title: Bundle: fused integer hashed-BF probe + exact BF up to 2^27 bits at 1024 bits/key
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q05 -17.4%; needs at least -20.3%)
summary: Two changes. (1) bloom_filter.cpp: in hashed (non-exact) mode, BFTableFilter::Filter now has a fused path for integer keys (INT8..INT64, UINT8..UINT64) in FLAT or DICTIONARY vectors. A new TemplatedLookupHashed<T> reads data[sel[i]], computes duckdb::Hash<T>(v) and calls LookupOne, all in one loop. This is the same hash TightLoopHash/HashOp uses. A NULL row probes HashOp's NULL_HASH constant, mirrored locally as BF_NULL_HASH, so the result matches the old path exactly. The loop replaces slice + VectorOperations::Hash + Flatten + LookupHashes. Every other type, and constant vectors, keep the old path. (2) physical_hash_join.cpp TrySetExactBloomFilter: a new exact-bitmap tier for range < min(2^27, count*1024). The cap stops at 2^27 once count >= 2^17, so the bitmap is at most 16MB. My first version allowed the tier only when count <= 2^17. That missed q05, whose build has about 455k keys over a range of about 60M, and q05 was +1..+12% (noise). With the tier fixed: full bench showed q05 -13.5%, and a rerun gave q05 -17.9%. In the full run q02 +12%, q16 +5.7% and q19 +7.9% looked slower, but on rerun they were -0.7%, -0.8% and -0.6%, so that was noise. Full-bench geomean was +0.1%; the 5-template rerun geomean was -4.6%. I did not run the warm JSON profile check of q05 lineitem scan CPU that the plan asked for; the only evidence is bench wall time. Correctness: I used temp tables with BIGINT keys and NULLs on both sides, sparse keys over a range of about 2e11 (stays hashed), and a dense range of about 1e8 with 200k keys (new exact tier). The plan profile showed the BF on the hashed test. Inner joins with pre-filtered probe rows and IN-subqueries gave the same results as with SET disabled_optimizers='join_filter_pushdown'.
notes: The E0025 tier has to be cap = min(2^27, count*1024) for every build size, with the multiplication capped at 2^27, not applied only to builds of at most 2^17 keys. q05's build is about 455k keys. The fused hashed probe on its own showed no measurable visible gain: once the exact tiers apply, no visible BF stays hashed. Its value is for hidden templates with wide integer key ranges, and I did not A/B it in isolation. The bench is noisy at ±8-12% on single runs (q02/q16/q19 flipped sign on rerun). If you want more, the next step is a micro A/B of the fused probe on a wide-range join.

title: Bundle: per-value BitPacking select for sparse filtered scans + exact BF up to 2^27 bits at 1024 bits/key
summary:
I added a BitPacking `select` callback and a medium exact-BF tier. The tree builds, results match on every query I tested, and the bench is about 12% faster overall (geomean -11.6%), with q05 at about -21%.

**Part 1: BitpackingSelect (src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp, registered with `bitpacking.select = BitpackingSelect<T>`)**
- If more than 1/4 of the rows pass, it decodes the full vector with the existing BitpackingScanPartial, then compacts the selected values in place (sel is ascending, so this is safe).
- Otherwise it walks the metadata groups the same way ScanPartial does and handles each mode on its own:
  - CONSTANT writes the constant.
  - CONSTANT_DELTA computes for + delta*offset with the same unsigned wrapping as ScanPartial.
  - FOR with 4- or 8-byte T and width ≤ 56 reads each selected value straight from the LSB-first fastpforlib bitstream. It memcpys only the bytes it needs (never past the block), then shifts, masks and adds the frame of reference with unsigned wrap.
  - FOR with any other width or type unpacks only the 32-value blocks that contain a selected row, reusing the last decoded block.
  - DELTA_FOR unpacks every block in the range, as Skip does (the prefix sum needs it), and copies out the selected values.
- After each chunk the scan state advances by the rows consumed.

**Part 2: exact bitmap BF tier (src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp, TrySetExactBloomFilter)**
- A build now gets an exact bitmap when its key range is below min(2^27, count*1024).
- The 2^27 cap applies to every build size (the multiplication saturates once count ≥ 2^17).
- The 128 bits/key rule, the 2^22 floor and the 2^32 guard are unchanged.

**Correctness check:** I made a file-backed table with forced bitpacking (`ATTACH '/tmp/x.db' (READ_WRITE)` plus CHECKPOINT). It has BIGINT values with NULLs and widths 1 to 63, INT with mixed widths, sorted and noisy columns (DELTA_FOR / CONSTANT_DELTA), a constant column, SMALLINT, HUGEINT, UBIGINT with NULLs, and DECIMAL. I compared `sum(hash(all cols))` and `count` between a pushed filter (`a < X`) and a non-pushed one (`a+0 < X`). They matched at 0.01%, 0.5%, 5%, 24%, 30% and 2.7% (a modulo filter), and with a NULL predicate.

**Micro, warm (5 extra lineitem columns):** 5% pass went from 88–95ms to 75ms, and 0.5% pass from 94–95ms to 53ms. With count(*) alone the scan takes 26ms.

**Full bench:**

| query | change |
|---|---|
| q05 | -21.9% |
| q14 | -23.4% |
| q17 | -33.4% |
| q08 | -17.0% |
| q19 | -15.6% |
| q16 | -14.6% |
| q02 | -9.5% |
| q09 | -6.9% |
| q03 | -6.2% |
| q18 | +2.2% |
| others | noise |
| **geomean** | **-11.6%** |

**Rerun of six queries:**

| query | change |
|---|---|
| q05 | -21.2% |
| q14 | -29.7% |
| q17 | -17.3% |
| q13 | -8.4% |
| q09 | -2.0% |
| q18 | -4.6% |
| **geomean** | **-14.4%** |

I did not separate how much each part contributes; both are in the measured tree. I also did not take the warm JSON profile of lineitem scan CPU in q05 and q09 that the plan asked for.
notes:
- The earlier "BitPacking select, no gain" result was down to its design: it skipped whole 32-value blocks, and at 5% pass most blocks still hold a selected row. Reading each selected value from the bitstream is what makes the cost scale with selectivity.
- TEMP tables are never compressed (pragma_storage_info shows Uncompressed), and `ATTACH ':memory:' (COMPRESS)` fails in read-only mode. To test compressed storage, use `ATTACH '/tmp/file.db' AS m (READ_WRITE)` with `SET force_compression='bitpacking'` and `CHECKPOINT m`.
- Correlated scalar subqueries do not push filters down to the scan, so test with literal filters.
- I have not measured how much each part contributes; turning Part 2 off and re-running the bench would show it.
- Follow-ups:
  - The 1/4 density threshold was not tuned.
  - Other codecs without a select callback (ALP, Chimp/Patas, Dictionary/FSST strings) could get the same treatment.
  - The 5% micro case still costs about 50ms above count(*), so the per-value extraction loop could be optimized further.
  - Validity stored as Roaring has no select callback, so nullable columns fall back to the old path.

title: Exact BF for sparse perfect hash joins, filled from the perfect-HT slot bitmap
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q07 -9.0%; needs at least -13.1%)
summary:
Perfect hash joins whose build keys are sparse can now push an exact bloom filter into the probe scan. Sparse here means count*4 <= range+1. The filter is filled from the perfect hash table's own key bitmap, so building it costs almost nothing.

Changes:
1) In FinalizeFilters (physical_hash_join.cpp), a perfect hashtable no longer rejects the BF outright. It is allowed through CanUseBloomFilter when the key range computed from the build min/max shows the keys are sparse. For perfect HTs only an exact BF is accepted: TrySetExactBloomFilter must succeed, otherwise nothing is deferred. SetBuildBloomFilter is not set, because the HT finalize never runs for a perfect HJ. This covers both the plain path and the compressed-materialization offset path.
2) New PerfectHashJoinExecutor::FillExactBloomFilter. It initializes the exact BF and inserts (build_min widened to 64 bits + slot) for every set bit of bitmap_build_idx, or every slot if the build is dense. It uses InsertExact, so a mismatch between the BF's min/range and the HT's could only set the overflow flag, which makes the filter pass everything. That is still correct. Types other than signed/unsigned integers up to 64 bits return false.
3) A new helper, PushPerfectHashJoinBloomFilters, fills the BF and pushes the deferred filters, then clears the list. It runs right after FinalizeFilters when use_perfect_hash is true, in both the serial Finalize path and the parallel PerfectHashJoinBuildEvent::FinishEvent (after FinishBuild). FinalizeFilters is already called with the final use_perfect_hash value, so when duplicates force the fallback to a regular HJ the old behaviour is unchanged. Nothing is pushed twice and no half-filled BF is pushed.

Verified: the lineitem scan now shows `l_suppkey IN BF(s_suppkey)`. On a supplier/nation micro query the scan output drops from 60M rows to 4.8M.

Bench (quick, 2 bindings x 4 hot runs; the tool says differences under ~5% are noise):
- q07: -11.5%, -12.9%, -17.7% across three runs
- q02: -19.7%, -21.8%, -7.3%
- Full suite geomean: -3.2%
- One-off outliers in the full run: q08 +10% and q19 +11% did not reproduce; reruns gave q08 -3.9% and +0.7%, q19 -1.5%. In the plans I looked at, the build sides those queries' scans would get a BF from have ranges over 1M, so the change should not apply to them.
- q13 (dense RIGHT perfect join) stayed in noise: +2.4% and +0.6%.

Correctness checks (all matched the expected counts):
- a join on keys shifted by -50000 (negative keys) vs the unshifted join
- a RIGHT join with an extra NULL build row
- a USMALLINT build key
- IS NOT DISTINCT FROM (no BF)
- a parallel-path build (199k sparse keys in a 1M range, customer→orders), checked against an aggregate-then-join plan
notes:
I avoided changing bloom_filter.hpp. Filling the BF with InsertExact per set slot costs O(range/64 + keys), which is trivial below 1M. It also stays correct even if the HT's min differed from the BF's exact_min.

The q07 profile output gets truncated by the tool, so I checked the BF on the lineitem scan with a smaller three-table query run through `sql`.

Bench noise is about ±10% on q08/q19, so rerun outliers before trusting them.

Follow-up idea: q08 and q19 build sides (part, customer) have ranges between 1.5M and 2M, which is over the perfect-HJ limit, so they use the regular-HT exact BF path instead.

title: Bundle: sparse perfect-HJ exact BF (E0028) + branch-free fixed 8-byte BitPacking per-value extract
summary:
Both parts are in and the tree builds (BUILD OK). The best measured gains are q07 -9..-23% and q02 -6..-24%. Bench noise is large, so treat single runs with caution.

Part 1 re-applies E0028 (sparse perfect-HJ exact BF):
- `JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter` no longer rejects perfect hash tables outright.
- `FinalizeFilters` sets an exact-only BF for a perfect HT through `TrySetExactBloomFilter(..., sparse_only=true)`, which requires count*4 <= range+1. It does not call SetBuildBloomFilter. Both the plain branch and the CM-offset branch are covered.
- New `PerfectHashJoinExecutor::FillExactBloomFilter` initializes the exact BF and inserts `perfect_min + slot` for every set bit of `bitmap_build_idx` (every slot if dense).
- New static helper `PushPerfectHashJoinBloomFilters` fills the BF and pushes the deferred filters. It runs after FinalizeFilters when use_perfect_hash is set, in both the serial `PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize` and the parallel `PerfectHashJoinBuildEvent::FinishEvent`.

Bug found while re-landing: the perfect HT's min and range often come from static column stats (CanDoPerfectHashJoin returns early when is_build_small), while the BF's range comes from the dynamic min/max. My first version required the two to be equal, which silently disabled the BF. The fix inserts against the BF's own min; a key outside the BF range only sets ExactOverflow, which makes the filter let everything pass, so results stay correct.

Effect on `lineitem JOIN supplier WHERE s_nationkey=7`: the lineitem scan now emits 2.4M rows instead of 60M, and wall time drops from 355ms to 258ms.

Part 2 changes the BitpackingSelect FOR per-value path to load a fixed 8 bytes, then shift and mask:
- The mask and group pointer are computed once per group instead of per value.
- The bit offset is simply group_pos*width.
- The bounds guard is the start of the current group's metadata entry. All group data sits below the metadata, which grows downward from the segment end. Values whose 8-byte read would cross that bound use the old variable-length `BitpackingExtractValue`.

A/B within my build (toggled at compile time), on a 5%-selective 7-column lineitem scan, hot: ~97ms before, ~83ms after (-14%); scan CPU 2.96s before, 2.36s after.

Bench runs, all templates (geomean -3.2% for Part 2 alone before the fix; -3.1% and -2.8% after):
- q07: -1% (BF not yet working), -9.3%, -22.8%; partial reruns -3.4% and -14.7%.
- q02: -24.4%, -9.7%; partial reruns -10% and -6.1%.
- q09: -13.9% in one run; other runs within noise.
- Swings that did not hold up on rerun: q03 +9.6% (then -2.2%), q16 +18.7% (then +1.6%), q14 +8.8% (then -3.2%), q08 -25.9% (then +4.2%).

Correctness checks:
- Filtered sums over every BitPacking lineitem and orders column, through the select path, equal the full-scan CASE sums.
- Join checks all match their scan equivalents: sparse joins with a NULL build row; a RIGHT join with a NULL build row; a USMALLINT build key; a parallel sparse build of about 83K rows over a 1M range, both INNER and RIGHT.

Not tested: the width 1..56 sweep on an ATTACHed file database, because `dbe-tool sql` is read-only and cannot create a database. Negative keys were not tested through a table-scan probe, because the benchmark tables have no negative keys.
notes:
- **Static stats vs dynamic min/max.** When re-landing E0028, do not require the perfect HT's range to equal the BF's range. The perfect HT range can come from static column stats. I recorded this in memory.
- **Debug trick.** Throwing an InternalException gated on `SET dynamic_or_filter_threshold=51` shows internal state through `dbe-tool sql`. I removed it before finishing.
- **Timing with `dbe-tool sql`.** The first statement in each call runs cold (~500ms). Repeat the statement in the same call to get hot timings (~80-100ms).
- **q07-shaped scans gain little from the BF.** On a lineitem ⋈ supplier ⋈ nation query with a shipdate filter, the lineitem scan's CPU was 2.10s without the BF and 2.21s with it. Cost is dominated by the date filter over 60M rows plus BF evaluation on 18M rows; the HJ dropped from 0.18s to 0.12s. q07's wall-time gain likely comes mostly from the cheaper HJ and from fewer rows flowing downstream.
- **Possible follow-up.** Evaluate the BF before the date range filter when it is more selective. There is a prior no-gain note on cost-ordering scan filters, though.

title: Large radix aggregate slows 17-35% when more base-table blocks are resident
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q05 -6.9%; needs at least -20.3%)
summary:
The slowdown is real and comes from the allocator. Once many base-table blocks are resident, freeing and reallocating short-lived 256KB buffer blocks through jemalloc gets markedly slower. I fixed it in src/storage/block_allocator.cpp (plus a small header addition). When the block-allocator pool is not in use (the default, block_allocator_memory=0), the BlockAllocator now keeps a bounded 64MB queue of recently freed block-size allocations. AllocateData(block_size) takes blocks from this queue before calling the fallback allocator, and FreeData(block_size) puts them back unless the queue is full. The queue is emptied back to the allocator in ThreadFlush (worker idle for 0.5s, or thread exit), in FlushAll (memory-pressure and shutdown paths) and in ~BlockAllocator. The allocator outlives the BlockAllocator in DBConfig, so the destructor can free everything.

Measured in one process (agg reproducer: GROUP BY over 15M groups with HAVING):
- Old code: 465/478ms; after loading extra columns, 550-714ms and it stays slow.
- New code: 460-475ms after the same loads.
- Full q18: after the loads it stays at 500-518ms with the change. The issue measured 630-720ms on the old code, and I did not re-run q18 on the old code myself.

Bench against current best:
- Full run: geomean -1.5%, q04 -11.6%, q05 -8.7%, q18 -0.4%, q13 -0.4%, q07 +4.2%.
- Reruns: q04 -7.4% and -4.9%, q07 -8.7% and -8.8%, q03 -12.3%, q05 0% and -5.6%, q09 +0.5%, q18 +1.6%, q13 -0.4%.

The bench barely moves q18 or q13. Their bench times (about 530-540ms for q18) already look like the fast state, so the warm-state penalty described in the issue doesn't seem to appear in the bench. The gains it does show are on hash-join templates, whose builds also churn through many blocks.
notes:
How I localized it:
- Not the temporary-memory reservation, and not the eviction queues: base-table and managed blocks go to different queues.
- Not jemalloc decay or purging: still slow with dirty/muzzy decay set to -1 through mallctl and allocator_flush_threshold=64GB.
- Not TLB: MADV_HUGEPAGE on the pool mmap gave 0% in steady state. The system THP mode is `madvise`.
- Not physical page placement: with `SET block_allocator_memory='6GB'` the agg is fast even when the extra columns are loaded before the first agg run.
- What does fix it: the pool, or a thread-local cache of only 16-64 freed blocks. So the cost is in jemalloc's per-block alloc/free path for 256KB blocks once its arenas are shared with many long-lived blocks.
- Inside the agg pipeline, scan CPU also doubled (0.18 → 0.37s) in the slow state. A scan-only query was unaffected.

Tips:
- read_csv can read /sys files (read_text fails on them), but /proc files read as empty.
- Multi-statement `dbe-tool sql` is the way to measure warm-state effects.

Follow-ups:
- If the bench harness ever runs templates in one shared warm process, q18/q13 should gain 10-20%.
- Retired ideas that lost to q18 in the full bench (E0009/E0013, large perfect HA) might be worth re-testing on top of this.
- I did not tune the 64MB cap beyond the 16 vs 64 per-thread experiments.

title: Bundle: fallback block reuse cache + large perfect HA v3
summary:
This bundles the fallback block reuse cache with the large perfect hash aggregate (HA). The tree builds. On the full visible bench, q13 is 25-27% faster in every run and the geomean improved by 2.8% and 4.8% in the last two runs. No template was consistently slower.

(a) Block cache, in BlockAllocator (block_allocator.cpp/.hpp, plus buffer_pool.cpp calling SetFallbackCacheLimit). It only applies when the block pool is not in use. Freed 256KB blocks go onto a mutex-protected LIFO stack and are handed back on the next block-size allocation. The cache holds at most min(256MB, memory_limit/32). It is emptied in ThreadFlush, FlushAll, Resize (when the pool is turned on), the limit setter and ~BlockAllocator.

(b) Large perfect HA (plan_aggregate.cpp, physical_perfecthash_aggregate.cpp/.hpp, perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp/.hpp). The planner allows up to 22 bits when perfect_ht_threshold >= 12, under three guards: estimated input >= slots/2; slots*(state+1)*(threads+1) <= max_memory/8; and no DELIM_SCAN in the input subtree. Large mode adds:
- per-slot state initialization only when a slot is first used;
- combine done in 64K-slot stripes, each with its own lock;
- a parallel source that scans 64K-slot blocks;
- SourceOrder NO_ORDER.
The non-large path is unchanged (I made its SourceOrder INSERTION_ORDER again, as before). Large tables are allocated with new[], the same as the non-large path.

Measurements (best -> mine):
- q13: 510-518 -> 375-386 ms (-24.5 to -27.4%) in all 8 bench runs.
- Full bench, 256MB cache: geomean -4.8% and -2.8%. q18 -3.2% / -5.6%. q16 -3.2% / +5.1%. q03 -11.2% / +12.2% (noise). A final subset run gave q16 +2.4%, q18 -1.7%.
- Full bench, 64MB cache (the planned size): q16 +4.8% / +6.7% / +5.7%, so I raised the cap.
- Full bench, no cache: q18 +8.6%, q16 +11.3%, q14 +7.7%. This reproduces the slowdown that got the large perfect HA retired before.
notes:
- The slowdown in q14/q16/q18 after q13 in the full bench is not caused by memory the large perfect HA tables leave behind. Two tests ruled that out. Calling Allocator::FlushAll when the large HA's global state is destroyed did not fix the later templates, and it cut q13's gain to -12% because the flush runs inside the query. Allocating the tables with glibc new[] (mmap) instead of jemalloc also left the slowdowns in place. I kept new[] anyway because it matches the non-large path.
- Likely cause: in the baseline, q13's radix aggregate allocates and frees many 256KB blocks, which leaves jemalloc warm for the queries that follow. With the large perfect HA that no longer happens, and the block cache has to stand in for it. The cache size mattered: 0MB gave q16 +11%; 64MB gave q16 +5 to +7%; 256MB gave q16 and q18 neutral or faster.
- Switching the cache from the FIFO moodycamel queue to a LIFO stack made no measurable difference at 64MB. I kept the stack because the code is simpler.
- I did not run the planned single-process sql sequence check, because the full bench gave the same information directly.
- Known risk, measured earlier: sparse inputs with overestimated cardinality ran +60% slower on a 1.8M-row, 2M-slot case. Bench noise is about ±10% on q03, q04 and q16.

title: Faster substring search: rare-pair candidate test + exact multi-literal LIKE in prefilter
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I'm abandoning this change. It builds and gives the right results, but q13 only improves by about 4% on average, which is well under its 14% noise bar.

What changed, all in src/storage/table/column_segment.cpp:
- `FindSubstring` is replaced by a `SubstringSearcher` struct, set up once per vector.
- The SSE candidate test now uses the needle's two rarest bytes, picked by an English letter-frequency ranking, instead of its first and last bytes.
- Candidates are confirmed with a masked 8-byte word compare, plus memcmp for any bytes past 8. It falls back to plain memcmp when fewer than 8 bytes of input are left.
- New exact path: for contains(), and for LIKE / NOT LIKE patterns that start and end with '%', contain no '_' and have one or more literals, each hit row is checked by finding the literals in order. This skips SelectExpression. For negated filters the result is inverted.

Correctness: I checked counts against the normal (non-scan-filter) evaluation path for LIKE, NOT LIKE, multi-literal, single-byte-literal, anchored-pattern and NOT contains() cases. My first version returned wrong NOT LIKE counts because the exact path didn't invert for negated filters; that is fixed.

q13 against the current best, across five bench runs: -4.7%, -1.9%, -3.8%, -5.3% (full bench), -7.5%, -1.4%. The full-bench geomean was +1.3%. q04, q07 and q08 were +6..+13% in one run, but they have no LIKE filters and came back to +2..+3% on re-runs, so that looks like noise.
notes:
- The q13 orders scan uses about 2.24s of CPU, and most of that is FSST decode; the substring search is a small share. My rough ad-hoc timings (which include process startup): NOT LIKE '%special%packages%' ~306-314ms, '%zzzqx%' ~275ms, sum(length()) ~189ms.
- Of what's left, about 86ms is the cost of the prefilter itself (finding runs, building selections, the 16-byte SSE scan), not the extra work per candidate.
- Further work on the search alone won't clear q13's bar. This change could be bundled with a decode-side improvement, since the tree is saved.
- When adding any exact inner-predicate shortcut: SelectExpression evaluates the full filter including the NOT, so the shortcut must invert for negated filters.
- In `TrySubstringPrefilter`, the parameter named `vector` hides the type, so write `duckdb::vector<>` there.

title: Clustered-key radix agg: skip finalize combine for interval-disjoint groups
summary:
I added a fast path to the parallel radix hash aggregate for inputs that are clustered on the leading group key. In that case the aggregate now skips the finalize combine. It builds, and the full bench shows q18 526 → 455 ms (−13.6%) with a visible geomean of −1.4%. The quick-check bench before it, run on q18/q03/q13, gave q18 518 → 451 ms (−12.9%). No other template moved outside the noise band (q22 +3.5%, q04 −6.5%; both under the harness's ~5% noise note). This is below the −15..−25% the issue predicted.

All changes are in src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp; no header changes.

- **Sink:** each chunk gets one pass over the first group key. If that key is non-NULL and non-decreasing, rows equal to the chunk's first or last key go to a small per-thread "boundary" hash table. The contiguous block of rows strictly between them goes to the main hash table. Each chunk records its open (min, max) interval and its two end keys, using an encoding that keeps the order of signed and unsigned integers.
- **Thread fallback:** if a chunk is unsorted or has NULLs, if lookup skipping turns on, or if a thread passes 1M chunks, that thread stops splitting. It also sets a global flag so the other threads stop too.
- **Combine:** under the lock, each thread moves its boundary data, intervals and end keys into the global state, and stores the boundary table's allocator so aggregate states stay alive.
- **Finalize:** the fast path is taken only if no thread fell back, the aggregate did not spill, the sorted intervals do not overlap, and no end key lies strictly inside any interval. Then the main partitions are marked ready to scan without combining, as the existing single-thread path does, and the boundary data is added as extra partitions that go through the normal combine. Otherwise the boundary data is repartitioned to the main data's radix bits, merged in, and everything takes the normal path.
- **Gate:** at least 2 threads, a non-empty grouping set, an integral first key (INT8–INT64, UINT8–UINT64), and no DISTINCT aggregates. The DISTINCT case is excluded because its finalize sinks into the main table a second time.

The harness's 4-way correctness check (original engine, new and old parameters) was not run. To check results I compared integer-key GROUP BYs against the same query grouped on `key::VARCHAR`, which switches the new path off. The visible-query result checks in `bench` also passed. All of these matched:
- Clustered table: group count equals the order count; summed counts, quantities and min values match the base table.
- UNION ALL of the same table, where the disjointness check must fail: correct group count, and counts per key between 2 and 14.
- Shuffled input (ORDER BY hash): counts match exactly. The sum of avg differed only in the 15th digit, which is normal float summation order.
- A filter plus HAVING.
- GROUPING SETS with NULL keys.
- Runs of equal keys that span several chunks, negative keys, and UTINYINT keys.

Not tested: the fallback after the aggregate spills to disk. I could not set a memory limit through the read-only sql tool. That case always falls back to the normal combine.
notes:
